questions.question: Define weathering and distinguish it from erosion, naming the three types of weathering.
questions.expected_answer: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place at or near the earth's surface by weather, water, chemicals and living things; erosion is the removal/transport of weathered material by water, wind, ice or gravity. Types: physical (mechanical) - breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing minerals; chemical - changes minerals into new substances; biological - by living things (physical or chemical). It is the first step in soil formation and landform development, and it damages buildings.

questions.question: Explain two processes of physical weathering and two of chemical weathering, with examples.
questions.expected_answer: Physical: frost action/freeze-thaw (water expands about 9% when frozen, wedging cracks; scree; Drakensberg); exfoliation/onion-skin (heating and cooling, pressure release; domes such as Paarl Rock); salt crystal growth; block disintegration along joints. Chemical: oxidation (iron minerals rust, red soils); carbonation (carbonic acid dissolves limestone - Cango, Sudwala caves, stalactites/stalagmites); hydrolysis (feldspar in granite to clay); solution; spheroidal weathering rounds boulders.

questions.question: Describe biological weathering and explain how climate influences the type and rate of weathering.
questions.expected_answer: Biological: roots widen cracks; burrowing animals (termites, worms, moles) expose fresh rock and mix soil; lichens and humic acids from decaying plants weather rock chemically. Climate: hot and wet - fast chemical weathering, deep soils (e.g. KwaZulu-Natal coast); hot and dry - physical weathering by temperature change and salt (Karoo, Namib); cold with freeze-thaw - frost action; cold and dry - slow. Rock type also matters (limestone vs hard quartzite/sandstone).
